title: Melting and solidifying: why chocolate melts in your hand but candle wax does not

summary.text: Put an ice cube, a piece of chocolate, some butter, some coconut oil and a bit of candle wax side by side. Which one melts first? Your child races them on a plate, then in a bowl of warm water, then near a candle flame. Each solid melts at its own warmth: ice and coconut oil in a warm room, chocolate and butter in warm water, and wax only near a flame. In the fridge, the melted chocolate, butter and oil set hard again. Melting turns a solid into a liquid. Solidifying turns it back.
summary.art: A steel plate with five small heaps in a row, each with a paper label: an ice cube in a small puddle, a runny spoonful of coconut oil, a soft blob of butter, a square of chocolate and a stub of white candle wax.

intro.hook: A square of chocolate melts on your tongue in a minute. A candle sits on the shelf all summer and never melts. Both are solids. Why does one melt so easily and the other not at all?
intro.text: Ice, chocolate, butter and wax all melt in the end. But they do not melt at the same warmth. You are going to race them and find out which one melts first, and which one needs the most warmth. Then you will cool them down and see what happens.
intro.art: A child holding a square of chocolate in one hand and a white candle in the other, looking from one to the other.

outcomes: By the end I can say that melting is a solid turning into a liquid, and solidifying is a liquid turning into a solid.
By the end I can say that freezing is the word for solidifying when it happens in the cold, like water turning into ice.
By the end I can show that different solids melt at different warmths, and put ice, chocolate and wax in order.
By the end I can show that melted chocolate, butter and coconut oil set solid again when they cool, and are still the same thing.
By the end I can say that warmth goes into a solid to melt it, and comes out of a liquid when it solidifies.
By the end I can guess first, give a reason, and then say what my test showed.

terms.meaning: To melt is to turn from a solid into a liquid when something gets warm enough.
terms.example: An ice cube melts into water on a plate. Chocolate melts in your mouth.
terms.art: An ice cube on a steel plate, half melted, sitting in its own small puddle.

terms.meaning: To solidify is to turn from a liquid into a solid when something cools down enough.
terms.example: Melted candle wax solidifies into a hard drop on a steel plate in a few seconds.
terms.art: White drops of candle wax that have set hard on a steel plate.

terms.meaning: To freeze is to solidify in the cold. We use this word most for water turning into ice.
terms.example: Water in an ice tray freezes into ice cubes in the freezer.
terms.art: An ice tray in a freezer, half of the squares still water and half white with ice.

terms.meaning: The melting point is the warmth at which a solid melts. Every substance has its own melting point.
terms.example: Ice melts at a low warmth. Candle wax needs much more warmth. Iron needs a furnace.
terms.art: A row of an ice cube, a chocolate square, a candle and an iron nail, with a small flame drawn bigger and bigger under each one.

terms.meaning: Temperature is how hot or cold something is. We measure it in degrees Celsius with a thermometer.
terms.example: Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius. Your body is about 37 degrees Celsius.
terms.art: A simple thermometer with a mark at 0 beside an ice cube and a mark at 37 beside a child's hand.

terms.meaning: A solid keeps its own shape. It does not flow.
terms.example: A square of chocolate from the fridge, a candle and an ice cube are solids.
terms.art: A chocolate square, a candle and an ice cube standing on a table, each keeping its own shape.

terms.meaning: A liquid flows and takes the shape of whatever holds it.
terms.example: Melted ghee, water and coconut oil on a hot day are liquids.
terms.art: Golden melted ghee being poured from a steel spoon into a katori.

terms.meaning: Wax is a soft solid that melts when it is quite hot. Candle wax is usually made from petroleum. Beeswax is made by honeybees.
terms.example: The wax of a candle melts into a clear pool just under the flame.
terms.art: A lit candle with a small clear pool of melted wax around the wick.

terms.meaning: A reversible change is one you can undo. Melting and solidifying are reversible changes.
terms.example: Chocolate melted in warm water sets solid again in the fridge, and it is still chocolate.
terms.art: Two arrows in a circle between a solid chocolate square and a puddle of melted chocolate.

explanations.concept: Melting: a solid turns into a liquid
explanations.context: This card explains what melting is.
explanations.definition: Melting is when a solid turns into a liquid because it has become warm enough.
explanations.description: In the melting race, the ice cube slowly became a puddle on the plate. The chocolate went soft, then runny, in the warm water. Nothing was added to them. They only got warmer.
examples: Ice turns into water on a plate.
Butter turns runny in a hot pan.
Kulfi drips down its stick on a hot day.
explanations.art: Three pictures in a row: an ice cube, a smaller ice cube in a puddle, and only a puddle.

explanations.concept: Solidifying and freezing: a liquid turns into a solid
explanations.context: This card explains what solidifying and freezing are.
explanations.definition: Solidifying is when a liquid turns into a solid because it has cooled down enough. Freezing is solidifying in the cold, like water turning into ice.
explanations.description: In the fridge, the melted chocolate, butter and coconut oil set hard again. A drop of candle wax set on a steel plate in a few seconds, because the plate is far cooler than a flame. Water stayed liquid in the fridge. It needs the much colder freezer to turn into ice.
examples: Water in an ice tray freezes in the freezer.
Hot ghee poured into a jar solidifies on a cold morning.
Melted wax solidifies as soon as it drips off a candle.
explanations.art: A steel katori of runny chocolate going into a fridge, and the same katori coming out with hard, set chocolate.

explanations.concept: Every solid melts at its own warmth
explanations.context: This card explains why the solids in the melting race did not all melt together.
explanations.definition: The melting point of a substance is the temperature at which it melts. Different substances have different melting points.
explanations.description: Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius, so it melts in almost any room. Coconut oil melts at about 24 degrees, so it is liquid on most warm days and solid on a cold morning. Butter and chocolate melt a little below the warmth of your body, so they melted in the warm water and in your mouth. Candle wax melts at a temperature much hotter than bath water, nearer hot tea, so it stayed hard until it was near the flame. Iron melts only in a furnace, at about 1,500 degrees.
examples: Chocolate and butter: a little below 37 degrees, the warmth of your body.
Candle wax: usually between about 45 and 70 degrees.
explanations.art: A tall thermometer with small pictures beside it at different heights: an ice cube at the bottom, a coconut oil bottle, a chocolate square, a candle higher up, and an iron nail in a glowing furnace at the very top.

explanations.concept: Melting and solidifying can be undone
explanations.context: This card explains why melted chocolate is still chocolate.
explanations.definition: A reversible change is a change that can be undone. When a substance melts and then solidifies again, it is still the same substance.
explanations.description: Your chocolate melted in warm water and set again in the fridge. It still tasted of chocolate. Ice that melts is still water, and you can freeze it again. Set chocolate may look dull or streaky, because its fat sets in a new pattern. It is still chocolate. A cooked dosa cannot turn back into batter, so cooking is not a reversible change.
examples: Water to ice to water, again and again.
Old candle stubs melted down and poured into a new candle.
Ghee that sets in winter and melts again on the stove.
explanations.art: A circle of two arrows: an ice cube melting into water, and water freezing back into an ice cube.

explanations.concept: Warmth goes in to melt a solid, and comes out when it solidifies
explanations.context: This card explains where the warmth goes when ice melts.
explanations.definition: A solid needs warmth to melt. That warmth comes from whatever is around it: the air, your hand or warm water. When a liquid solidifies, it gives out warmth to what is around it.
explanations.description: Hold an ice cube, and your hand gets cold. Warmth flows out of your hand into the ice and melts it. The ice in a glass of nimbu pani cools the drink in the same way. It takes a lot of warmth to melt ice, so an ice cube lasts a long time, even in a warm room. Warmth always flows from the warmer thing to the cooler thing.
examples: Ice cools a glass of buttermilk as it melts.
Your hand feels cold when you hold ice.
A bowl of warm water melted the chocolate quickly.
explanations.art: A child's hand holding an ice cube, with small red arrows going from the hand into the ice.

explanations.concept: What happens inside a solid when it melts
explanations.context: This card explains what melting looks like if we could zoom in very far.
explanations.definition: Everything is made of tiny particles, far too small to see. In a solid they hold each other in place. In a liquid they hold on loosely and slide past each other.
explanations.description: The tiny particles of a solid are always jiggling, even when the solid sits still. Warm them, and they jiggle harder. At the melting point they jiggle so hard that they slide past each other, and the solid flows as a liquid. Cool them, and they slow down and settle back into place. Different substances have different particles, held with different strength, so each one needs its own warmth to melt.
examples: Ice particles slide apart at 0 degrees Celsius.
Wax particles need a candle flame's warmth to slide apart.
explanations.art: A zoom-in circle: on the left, tiny balls in neat rows; on the right, the same balls jumbled and sliding.

agreed.text: Melting turns a solid into a liquid, and solidifying turns a liquid into a solid.
agreed.evidence: In the melting race, the ice became water and the chocolate became runny. In the fridge, the melted chocolate and butter set hard again.

agreed.text: Different substances melt at different temperatures.
agreed.evidence: On the same plate, the coconut oil melted in minutes, the chocolate stayed hard, and the wax melted only near a candle flame.

agreed.text: Pure water freezes and ice melts at the same temperature, 0 degrees Celsius.
agreed.evidence: Thermometers in melting ice always read 0 degrees, however much ice there is. This is why the Celsius scale uses it as its zero.

agreed.text: A substance that melts and solidifies again is still the same substance.
agreed.evidence: Chocolate melted and set again still tastes of chocolate. Water frozen and melted many times is still water.

challenging.claim: Hot water can freeze faster than cold water.
challenging.who: Erasto Mpemba, a schoolboy in Tanzania, who noticed it in 1963 while making ice cream. He and the physicist Denis Osborne wrote about it in 1969.
challenging.for: Mpemba saw his hot ice cream mix freeze before his friends' cold mix. Some later tests have found the same thing.
challenging.against: Other careful tests found that hot water does not freeze faster when everything else is kept the same. The result changes with the container and the freezer.
challenging.context: This card is about a surprising idea from a Tanzanian schoolboy that scientists still argue about.

challenging.claim: Ice is slippery because your weight squeezes it and melts it.
challenging.who: An explanation found in many older books.
challenging.for: Squeezing ice does make it melt at a slightly lower temperature.
challenging.against: Scientists worked out that a person's weight does not squeeze hard enough to melt much ice. Ice is slippery even when you only touch it lightly. Most now think the surface of ice has a very thin wet layer of its own.
challenging.context: This card is about why ice is slippery.

challenging.claim: When ice melts, cold flows out of the ice into your hand.
challenging.for: Your hand feels cold when you hold ice, so it seems as if cold has come into it.
challenging.against: Scientists describe it the other way round. Warmth flows from your warm hand into the ice and melts it. Your hand feels cold because it has lost warmth.
challenging.context: This card is about what really moves when you hold an ice cube.

challenging.claim: Chocolate that has melted and set again is spoiled.
challenging.for: Set chocolate can look dull or have white streaks on top.
challenging.against: The streaks are the fat in the chocolate, set in a different pattern. It is the same chocolate and is safe to eat if it was clean and stored well.
challenging.context: This card is about chocolate that melts and sets again.

big_questions.q: Coconut oil is a liquid in Kochi and a solid on a winter morning in Delhi. So is coconut oil a solid or a liquid?
big_questions.hint: Does the answer depend on the oil, or on the place, or on both?

big_questions.q: Why does chocolate melt in your mouth but not in its wrapper on the shelf?
big_questions.hint: Which is warmer: the inside of your mouth or the room?

big_questions.q: When ice melts in your hand, where does the warmth come from? Where does it go?
big_questions.hint: Why does your hand feel cold afterwards?

big_questions.q: Rocks melt deep inside the Earth and come out of volcanoes as lava. Is there anything that never melts?
big_questions.hint: Think of how hot the inside of the Sun is.

big_questions.q: If the ice on the Himalayas melts, where does the water go?
big_questions.hint: Think of the rivers that start in the mountains.

how_we_found_out.story: About 260 years ago, people thought ice melted the moment it became just a little warmer than freezing. They thought only a tiny bit of warmth was needed. Joseph Black, a scientist in Glasgow, Scotland, tested this around 1761. He set out two glass containers in a warm room. One held ice. The other held the same amount of very cold water, only just above freezing. He watched how fast each one warmed up. The cold water warmed up by several degrees in about half an hour. The ice took about ten hours to melt and warm up by the same amount. The whole time it was melting, the ice and its water stayed at freezing. So all that warmth from the room had gone into melting the ice, not into warming it. Black showed that melting needs a lot of warmth, even though a thermometer shows no change. That is why an ice cube lasts so long in a warm room, and why snow on mountains melts slowly in spring.
how_we_found_out.who: Joseph Black, a Scottish doctor and scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That ice melts with only a tiny bit of warmth, as soon as it is a little above freezing. Black showed that ice soaks up a lot of warmth while it melts, without getting any warmer.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in 1700s clothes in a warm room looking at two glass flasks, one full of ice and one full of water, with a clock on the wall.

story.title: The Coconut Oil That Turned White
story.note: Lakshmi, Ishita, Sreeja Ammayi and Appa are made up. Ammayi is a Malayalam word for an aunt. Coconut oil really does turn white and solid in a Delhi winter, because it melts at about 24 degrees Celsius.
text: Lakshmi was eight, and she lived in Kochi, in Kerala. In Kochi it is warm all year. Every morning, her Amma rubbed a little coconut oil into Lakshmi's hair. The oil came out of the bottle clear and golden, like honey.

In January, Lakshmi and her Appa took a train to Delhi. They were going to stay with Sreeja Ammayi, Appa's sister, and her daughter Ishita, who was six. Amma packed a bottle of coconut oil in Lakshmi's bag.
Delhi in January was cold. Lakshmi had never felt cold like it. Fog hung over the road in the mornings. She wore two sweaters and a woolly cap, and she could see her breath in the air.
On the first morning, Lakshmi took out her bottle of coconut oil. She tipped it over her hand. Nothing came out. She shook it. Still nothing.
She held the bottle up to the window. The oil was not golden any more. It was white, like a block of soap, and it was hard.
"Appa!" she called. "My coconut oil has gone bad!"
Appa came and looked. He frowned. "It must have spoiled on the train," he said. "We had better throw it away and buy a new bottle."
Ishita came running in her pyjamas. "Ours does that too," she said. "Every winter."
Sreeja Ammayi was in the kitchen, making poha for breakfast. She came to the door with a spoon in her hand. She smiled when she saw the white bottle.
"Don't throw it away," she said. "Nothing is wrong with it. Lakshmi, how warm is it in Kochi in January?"
"Warm," said Lakshmi. "Always warm."
"And how warm is it here?"
Lakshmi pulled her cap down over her ears. "Cold," she said.
Sreeja Ammayi filled a steel bowl with warm water from the geyser. It was as warm as bath water. "Put the bottle in here," she said, "and watch."

Lakshmi stood the bottle in the warm water. Ishita and Appa leaned in close. At first, nothing happened. Then, at the bottom of the bottle, a thin line of clear, golden oil appeared. It grew. The white block began to shrink from the edges, and float in the clear oil. After a few minutes the white block was gone. The bottle was full of golden oil again, just like in Kochi.
"It melted!" said Ishita.
"It was solid because it was cold," said Lakshmi slowly. "Coconut oil goes solid in the cold and liquid when it is warm. Like ice and water."

"That's right," said Sreeja Ammayi. "Coconut oil has its own melting point. It melts at a warmth a bit cooler than a Kochi day, and warmer than a Delhi morning in January. In Kochi it is nearly always warmer than that, so you only ever see it as a liquid."
Appa scratched his head. "I grew up in Kochi too," he said. "I have never once seen coconut oil turn white."
"Then today you learned something from your daughter," said Sreeja Ammayi.
Lakshmi took the bottle out of the water and rubbed the oil into her hair. Then she had an idea. She poured a little oil into a small steel katori and put it on the cold window sill.
After breakfast, she ran to look. The oil in the katori had turned white and hard again. Ishita poked it with her finger. Her warm finger made a small, shiny dip where the oil had melted.
"Your finger melted it," said Lakshmi. "Your finger is warmer than the window."
That night, Lakshmi wrote in her notebook: "Coconut oil is the same oil in Kochi and in Delhi. In Kochi it is a liquid. In Delhi in winter it is a solid. It only depends on how warm it is."
story.epiphany: Lakshmi saw that her coconut oil had not gone bad. It was the same oil, solid in the cold and liquid in the warm. Whether it was a solid or a liquid depended on how warm it was around it.
ask: Why did Lakshmi's coconut oil turn white and hard in Delhi?
What did Sreeja Ammayi do to make it golden again?
Why did Ishita's finger make a shiny dip in the oil?
Where in your home could you make coconut oil go solid?

A bottle of half-white, half-golden coconut oil standing in a steel bowl of warm water, with two girls and a man leaning in to watch.

experiments.title: The Melting Race: which solid melts first?
experiments.context: In this experiment you race five solids: an ice cube, a square of chocolate, a little butter, a little coconut oil and a piece of candle wax. First they sit on a plate in the room. Then they float in a bowl of warm water. Last, a grown-up lights a candle. Then you cool them in the fridge.
experiments.question: Do all solids melt at the same warmth? Which one melts first, and which one needs the most warmth?
experiments.predict: Look at the five solids. Which one will melt first on the plate? Which will melt last? Will any of them not melt at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each solid is about the same small size, about as big as the tip of your thumb. They all sit on the same plate, in the same room, for the same time. In the warm water, they all float in the same bowl.
results_table: Melting on the plate after 10 minutes?

materials.item: a steel plate, and five small steel katoris or bottle caps that float
one ice cube from the freezer
one small square of plain chocolate, from any chocolate bar
half a teaspoon of butter, or ghee, kept in the fridge
half a teaspoon of coconut oil, set hard in the fridge for an hour beforehand
a short candle, and a piece of wax about as big as your thumb tip (scrape it off the candle, or use a wax crayon)
a wide steel bowl or a vessel, and warm water as warm as a bath
five small paper slips and a pencil, to label the solids
matches, used only by a grown-up
a clock or a phone timer

experiments.safety: A grown-up lights and holds the candle, and keeps it away from hair, cloth and paper. Melted wax near the flame is hot, so nobody touches the pool. The warm water must be only as warm as a bath, so your child can keep a finger in it.

schedule.what: Guess the order. Watch the five solids on a plate for 10 minutes, then in warm water, then see wax melt near a flame. Put them in the fridge for 20 minutes and look again.

experiments.record: Write your guess for the order at the top. Fill in the table with a tick or a cross. Draw what each solid looked like after the warm water.

setup.art: A child looking closely at the plate, with a phone timer beside it showing 10 minutes.
setup.caption: 2. Watch them for 10 minutes. Which ones start to melt?

setup.caption: 3. Float them in warm water. Which ones melt now?

setup.art: A grown-up holding a lit candle upright, with a clear pool of melted wax around the wick.

flow.context: This is the first step of the melting race. You set out the five solids and guess.
flow.do: 1. Put the five solids in a row on the steel plate. 2. Your child writes a label for each one. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Here are five solids: ice, chocolate, butter, coconut oil and wax. They will all sit in the same room. Which one will melt first? Which one last? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the five solids. Which will melt first? Which will melt last? Say why.

ask.q: Which one will melt first? Why?
good: The ice, because it is cold and melts fast.
The butter, because it is soft.
The chocolate, because it melts in my mouth.

flow.parent: Take the coconut oil and butter out of the fridge just now, so they start hard. Don't say which guess is right. Many children say ice will melt first. Write the guessed order at the top of the table.

flow.context: In this step of the melting race, the five solids sit on a plate in the room.
flow.do: 1. Leave the plate on a table, out of the sun and away from the fan. 2. Every 2 minutes, look closely together. 3. Tick each one that has started to melt.
flow.say: Look closely. Is anything wet, shiny or runny? That means it has started to melt. Let's look again every 2 minutes.
flow.kid: Look at each solid every 2 minutes. Is it wet, shiny or runny? Tick it.

ask.q: Which ones have started to melt? Which ones still look hard?
good: The ice and the coconut oil are melting.
The wax looks the same as before.

flow.parent: In most Indian homes, which are warmer than 24 degrees, the coconut oil turns runny within about 10 minutes. The ice starts melting at once but takes much longer to finish. The butter goes soft and shiny. The wax stays hard. The chocolate usually stays hard too, but in a very hot kitchen it may go soft at the edges. In a cold room, the coconut oil may stay solid, and that is a real result too.

flow.context: In this step of the melting race, the solids float in a bowl of warm water.
flow.do: 1. Fill the wide bowl with water as warm as a bath. 2. Your child tests it with a finger. 3. Put each solid in its own katori (scrape the runny ones in), and float the katoris on the water. 4. Watch for 5 minutes.
flow.say: This water is as warm as a bath. Now which ones will melt? Will the wax melt too? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Float each solid on the warm water. Watch for 5 minutes. Which ones melt now?

ask.q: What happened to the chocolate and the butter?
good: They went runny.
The chocolate melted in the warm water.

ask.q: What happened to the wax?
good: Nothing. It is still hard.
It did not melt in the warm water.

flow.parent: The chocolate and butter melt in a few minutes, because bath water is warmer than their melting points. The wax stays hard. Let your child press it with a finger to check. Don't explain yet. Melted chocolate may keep its square shape until you poke it, so press it to check.

check.q: The chocolate melted in the warm water, but the wax did not. Why?
options: Wax needs more warmth to melt than chocolate
check.why: Each solid has its own melting point. Bath water is warm enough for chocolate, but wax needs much more warmth. Picking 'wax never melts' is a good guess to test in the next step.

flow.context: In this step of the melting race, a grown-up lights a candle to see if wax can melt.
flow.do: 1. Light the candle and hold it upright on a steel plate. 2. Your child watches from an arm's length away. 3. After two or three minutes, point to the wax around the wick. 4. Blow it out.
flow.say: Look just under the flame. What is happening to the wax there? Now I will blow it out. Watch the pool.
flow.kid: Watch from an arm's length. Look under the flame. What is the wax doing?

ask.q: Did the wax melt?
good: Yes, it made a clear pool under the flame.
It melted when it was very hot.
It went white and hard again when the flame went out.

flow.parent: A small pool of clear liquid wax forms around the wick within two or three minutes. After you blow it out, the pool turns white and hard in about a minute. So wax does melt, but only near a flame.

flow.context: In this step of the melting race, you cool the melted solids in the fridge.
flow.do: 1. Put the katoris of melted chocolate, butter, coconut oil and ice water in the fridge. 2. Ask the question below. 3. Set a timer for 20 minutes.
flow.say: These have all melted. What will they be like after 20 minutes in the fridge? Will the water turn back into ice? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put the melted ones in the fridge. What will happen? Guess, and say why.
flow.wait: Leave them in the fridge for 20 minutes.
flow.parent: Use the main part of the fridge, not the freezer. That way your child can see that water needs much more cold than the others.

flow.context: This is the last step of the melting race. You look in the fridge and say what you found.
flow.do: 1. Take out the katoris after 20 minutes. 2. Your child presses each one with a finger. 3. Fill in the last column. 4. Ask the three questions below.
flow.say: Which ones are solid again? Which one is still a liquid? Now tell me: what did you think, what did you see, and why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Press each one. Which are hard again? Which is still runny? What did you find out?

ask.q: Which ones solidified in the fridge?
good: The chocolate, the butter and the coconut oil went hard again.
The water stayed water.

ask.q: Why did the water not freeze?
good: The fridge is not cold enough for water.
Water needs the freezer.

ask.q: What did the race show?
good: Each one melts at a different warmth.
Ice and coconut oil melt easily, wax needs a flame.

flow.parent: A strong answer says that each solid melted at its own warmth, and that they solidified again when cooled. Then read the explanation cards together.

check.q: In the fridge, the chocolate went hard but the water stayed liquid. What does that show?
options: Water needs more cold to solidify than chocolate
The chocolate was not really melted
check.why: Chocolate solidifies a little below the warmth of your body, so the fridge is cold enough. Water freezes only at 0 degrees Celsius, so it needs the freezer.

experiments.title: The Freezer Watch: where does the ice start, and which cup freezes first?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put the same amount of water in a steel tumbler and in a plastic tumbler, and put both in the freezer. You look every 30 minutes to see where the ice starts, and which one freezes first.
experiments.question: When water freezes, where does the ice start: at the top, the bottom, the sides or the middle? Does a steel tumbler freeze faster than a plastic one?
experiments.predict: Where do you think the first ice will appear? Which tumbler will freeze first, the steel one or the plastic one? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both tumblers are about the same size, with the same amount of water from the same jug. They go into the freezer at the same time, side by side, and we look at both at the same times.
results_table: Steel tumbler: where is the ice?
Plastic tumbler: where is the ice?

materials.item: a small steel tumbler
a plastic tumbler or cup of about the same size
water from the same jug, the same amount in each (about half a tumbler)
space in the freezer
a steel spoon, to tap the ice gently
a clock or a phone timer

schedule.what: Fill both tumblers, guess, and put them in the freezer. Look every 30 minutes for about 3 hours, 2 or 3 minutes each time, and write down where the ice is.

experiments.record: Draw both tumblers at each look. Colour the ice blue and leave the water white.

setup.art: A steel tumbler and a plastic tumbler side by side, each half full of water.
setup.caption: 1. Put the same amount of water in each tumbler.

setup.art: The two tumblers standing side by side on a freezer shelf.
setup.caption: 2. Put them in the freezer side by side.

setup.art: Looking down into a tumbler: a thin white ring of ice around the edge and a thin skin on top, with water in the middle.
setup.caption: 3. Every 30 minutes, look. Where is the ice?

setup.art: A child gently tapping the top of the ice in a tumbler with a steel spoon.
setup.caption: 4. Tap gently with a spoon. Is it ice all the way down?

flow.context: This is the first step of the freezer watch. You fill the tumblers and guess.
flow.do: 1. Pour the same amount of water into both tumblers. 2. Ask the questions below. 3. Put both in the freezer, side by side.
flow.say: Where will the first ice appear: at the top, the bottom, the sides or the middle? Which tumbler will freeze first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Where will the ice start? Which tumbler will freeze first? Say why.

ask.q: Where will the ice start? Why?
good: At the bottom, because ice is heavy.
In the middle.
At the top, because the cold air touches it.

flow.parent: Write the guesses down. Don't say if they are right. Many children guess the bottom or the middle.

flow.context: In this step of the freezer watch, you look at the tumblers every 30 minutes.
flow.do: 1. Every 30 minutes, open the freezer and look at both tumblers. 2. Your child draws where the ice is. 3. Close the freezer quickly each time.
flow.say: Look from the top and from the side. Is there ice yet? Where is it?
flow.kid: Look at both tumblers. Where is the ice? Draw it. Close the freezer fast.

ask.q: Where did the ice start?
good: A thin skin on the top.
A ring round the edge, next to the cup.
The middle is still water.

flow.parent: Ice usually forms first as a thin skin on top and a ring round the sides, because those parts touch the cold air and the cold cup. The middle freezes last. The steel tumbler usually freezes first, because steel lets warmth out of the water faster than plastic. Freezers vary, so it may take 2 to 4 hours, and the two tumblers may freeze at nearly the same time. That is a real result too.

flow.context: This is the last step of the freezer watch. You tap the ice and say what you found.
flow.do: 1. When one tumbler is mostly frozen, take both out. 2. Your child taps the top gently with the spoon. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Which one froze first? Where did the ice start? Why do you think the middle froze last?
flow.kid: Tap the ice gently. Which froze first? Where did the ice start?

ask.q: Why did the ice start at the top and the sides?
good: They touch the cold.
The cold air and the cold cup took the warmth out there first.

ask.q: Why did the steel tumbler freeze first?
good: Steel gets cold quickly.
Warmth goes out through steel faster.

flow.parent: A strong answer says the water froze first where it lost its warmth first: next to the cold air and the cold cup. Steel lets warmth pass through it more easily than plastic.

check.q: In the freezer, where does ice usually start in a tumbler of water?
options: At the top and round the sides
check.why: The top touches the cold air and the sides touch the cold cup, so warmth leaves the water there first. The middle is last to lose its warmth.

experiments.safety: Cold steel can stick to a wet finger. Dry your hands and touch the tumblers only on the outside, with a cloth.

activities.title: Melt It on Your Tongue: chocolate or ice?
activities.context: In this activity you hold a small piece of chocolate on your tongue without chewing, then a small chip of ice. You notice what happens to each one, and which melts first.

materials.item: one small piece of chocolate, about the size of a fingernail
one small chip of ice, about the same size
a glass of water to drink afterwards

schedule.what: Hold a piece of chocolate on your tongue without chewing. Then a chip of ice. Say what you noticed.

activities.record: Draw the chocolate before and after it was on your tongue.

setup.art: A small square of chocolate and a small chip of ice side by side on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. Get a small piece of chocolate and a small chip of ice.

setup.art: A child with her eyes closed and her mouth shut, holding something still on her tongue.
setup.caption: 2. Hold it on your tongue. Don't chew. What happens?

flow.do: 1. Give your child the chocolate. 2. Ask them to hold it on their tongue and not chew. 3. Ask the questions below after a minute.
flow.say: Put the chocolate on your tongue, but don't chew it. Keep your mouth closed. What is happening to it?
flow.kid: Put the chocolate on your tongue. Don't chew. What is happening?

ask.q: What happened to the chocolate?
good: It went soft.
It turned runny.
It melted in my mouth.

flow.parent: Chocolate melts a little below the warmth of the inside of your mouth, so it turns runny within a minute. A child who has diabetes or cannot eat chocolate can use a little cold butter on the tip of a spoon instead.

flow.do: 1. Give your child the chip of ice. 2. Ask them to hold it on their tongue in the same way. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Now the ice. Hold it the same way. Which one melted faster? Where did the warmth to melt them come from?
flow.kid: Now hold the ice on your tongue. Did it melt? Which melted first?

ask.q: Where did the warmth come from?
good: From my mouth.
From my tongue, because I am warm.

flow.parent: Both melt. The ice makes your tongue feel cold, because warmth is leaving your tongue to melt it. Don't explain melting points yet. The melting race comes next.

activities.title: Wax Drops: watch hot wax turn solid
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up lets drops of melted wax fall from a candle onto a steel plate and into a katori of cold water. You watch how fast the liquid wax turns into a solid.

materials.item: a candle, and matches used only by a grown-up
a steel plate
a steel katori of cold water

activities.safety: A grown-up lights and holds the candle. Melted wax is hot, so let each drop sit for 10 seconds before your child touches it. Keep hair, cloth and paper away from the flame. Keep your face back when drops fall into the water.

schedule.what: A grown-up drips melted wax onto a plate and into cold water. Watch how fast it turns solid, then peel off the drops.

activities.record: Stick two wax drops in your notebook with tape. Write how many seconds it took for them to turn white.

setup.art: A grown-up tilting a lit candle over a steel plate so that a drop of clear wax falls onto it.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up tips the candle so a drop falls on the plate.

setup.art: Small round white wax drops on a steel plate, and some floating in a katori of water.
setup.caption: 2. Count how long the drop takes to turn white and hard.

setup.art: A child's fingers peeling a small round wax drop off a steel plate.
setup.caption: 3. Peel off a drop. Is it a solid now?

flow.do: 1. Light the candle. 2. Wait two or three minutes for a pool of wax to form. 3. Tip the candle gently so one drop falls on the plate. 4. Your child counts the seconds until it turns white.
flow.say: Look at the drop as it lands. It is clear and runny. Count with me. When does it turn white?
flow.kid: Watch the drop land. Count the seconds. When does it turn white?

ask.q: How many seconds did it take to turn white?
good: About 3 seconds.
Very fast, less than 10 seconds.

flow.parent: Each small drop goes from clear to white in a few seconds, as it cools and solidifies.

flow.do: 1. Now let a few drops fall into the katori of cold water. 2. Blow out the candle. 3. Your child fishes out a drop and feels it.
flow.say: Watch the drops land in the water. Did they turn white faster or slower? Now feel one. Is it a solid or a liquid?
flow.kid: Watch the drops fall in the water. Fish one out. Feel it.

ask.q: Why did the wax turn solid so fast?
good: The plate and the water are much cooler than the flame.
Wax goes solid when it cools.

flow.parent: In cold water the drops set almost at once, into little flat discs. The wax melted near the flame and solidified as soon as it cooled.

flow.do: 1. Your child peels a drop off the plate. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: This was a liquid a minute ago. What is it now? Could we melt it again?
flow.kid: Peel off a drop. It was a liquid before. What is it now?

ask.q: Could you melt it again?
good: Yes, near the flame.
Yes, melting can be undone.

activities.title: The Home Hunt: what melts, and where?
activities.context: In this activity you look around the kitchen for solids that melt. You sort them by where they would melt: in the room, in your warm hand, on the stove, or never in your home.

materials.item: a sheet of paper with four columns: in the room, in my hand, on the stove, never at home
a pencil

schedule.what: Hunt in the kitchen and fridge for solids. Sort them by where they would melt.

activities.record: Fill in the four columns with the things you found.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with four columns headed in the room, in my hand, on the stove, never at home.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the four columns.

setup.art: A child looking into an open fridge at a butter box, a jar of ghee and an ice tray.
setup.caption: 2. Look in the fridge and the kitchen. Where would each thing melt?

flow.do: 1. Walk round the kitchen together. 2. Look in the fridge too. 3. For each solid, your child guesses where it would melt, and writes or draws it in a column.
flow.say: Look at the ghee jar. Is it solid or liquid today? Where would it melt? What about the steel tumbler? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Find solids in the kitchen. Where would each one melt? Put it in a column.

ask.q: Which things would never melt in our home?
good: The steel tumbler.
The stone grinder.
The glass bottle.

flow.parent: Ghee, butter, coconut oil and ice cream melt easily. Jaggery and sugar go runny on the stove. Steel, glass and stone melt only in a furnace, far hotter than any kitchen. Don't heat anything to test it.

flow.do: 1. Look at the four columns together. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at your columns. Which column has the most things? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which column has the most things? Why?

ask.q: Is the ghee in our home solid or liquid today?
good: Solid, because it is cold today.
Liquid, because it is hot today.

activities.title: Lift an Ice Cube with a Thread
activities.context: In this activity you lay a piece of thread across an ice cube, sprinkle a little salt on it, and wait. Then you try to lift the ice cube with the thread.

materials.item: an ice cube in a small katori of water
a piece of cotton thread, about as long as your arm, wetted
a pinch of salt

schedule.what: Lay a wet thread on an ice cube, sprinkle salt on it, wait a minute, and lift the ice cube.

activities.record: Draw the ice cube hanging from the thread.

setup.art: An ice cube floating in a katori of water, with a wet thread lying across the top.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a wet thread across the top of the ice cube.

setup.art: A child sprinkling a pinch of salt onto the thread on the ice cube.
setup.caption: 2. Sprinkle a pinch of salt on the thread. Wait one minute.

setup.art: An ice cube hanging from a thread held up by a child's fingers.
setup.caption: 3. Lift the thread. Does the ice come too?

flow.do: 1. Your child tries to lift the ice cube with the thread, without salt. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Lay the thread on the ice and lift it. Did the ice come up? Now we will add a little salt. What do you think will happen? Why?
flow.kid: Lift the thread. Did the ice come up? Now guess what salt will do.

ask.q: What will the salt do? Why?
good: It will make the ice melt.
It will make the thread stick.

flow.do: 1. Lay the thread across the ice again. 2. Your child sprinkles a pinch of salt on it. 3. Count slowly to 60. 4. Your child lifts the thread gently.
flow.say: Count to 60 with me. Now lift slowly. What happens?
flow.kid: Sprinkle salt on the thread. Count to 60. Lift slowly.

ask.q: What happened?
good: The ice came up with the thread.
The thread stuck into the ice.

flow.parent: Salt makes the ice melt a little round the thread, even in the cold. Then the water freezes again over the thread and holds it. If it does not lift, wait another minute and add one more small pinch.

flow.do: 1. Look closely at the thread in the ice. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look where the thread is. The salt melted the ice a little, then the water froze again. Can you see the thread inside the ice?
flow.kid: Look at the thread. Is it inside the ice now?

ask.q: Why do kulfi sellers pack ice with salt?
good: Salty ice gets colder.
It keeps the kulfi frozen.

flow.parent: Ice mixed with salt gets colder than plain ice. Kulfi makers have long used ice and salt round their moulds to freeze kulfi.

games.title: Melt or Set? a snap card game
games.context: This is a quick card game. Each card shows a change. You shout 'Melt!' if a solid is turning into a liquid, or 'Set!' if a liquid is turning into a solid.

items.f: Kulfi dripping down its stick on a hot day
items.b: Melt. The solid kulfi turns into a liquid.

items.f: Water in an ice tray turning into ice cubes
items.b: Set. Water freezes into a solid.

items.f: Ghee in a jar going hard on a cold morning
items.b: Set. Liquid ghee solidifies when it cools.

items.f: Butter going runny in a hot pan
items.b: Melt. Solid butter turns into a liquid.

items.f: A candle making a clear pool round its wick
items.b: Melt. The flame melts the wax.

items.f: A drop of candle wax turning white on a plate
items.b: Set. The wax cools and solidifies.

items.f: Chocolate going soft in your pocket
items.b: Melt. Your body warms the chocolate.

items.f: Coconut oil turning white in a Delhi winter
items.b: Set. Coconut oil solidifies in the cold.

items.f: Snow on the Himalayas turning into streams in spring
items.b: Melt. The warm spring sun melts the snow.

items.f: Melted chocolate setting hard in the fridge
items.b: Set. The chocolate cools and solidifies.

items.f: Hailstones disappearing on a warm road
items.b: Melt. Hailstones are ice, and the warm road melts them.

items.f: Mango juice in a cup turning into an ice lolly
items.b: Set. The juice freezes in the freezer.

items.f: An ice cube shrinking in a glass of buttermilk
items.b: Melt. The buttermilk warms the ice.

items.f: Hot red lava turning into black rock
items.b: Set. Lava is melted rock. It solidifies as it cools.

items.f: Melted jaggery syrup setting into chikki
items.b: Set. The hot syrup cools and goes hard.

items.f: A crayon left on a hot window sill in May going soft and bendy
items.b: Melt. Crayons are made of wax, and strong sun can soften them.

rules: Cut out the 16 cards. Shuffle them and put them face down in a pile.
One player turns over the top card and reads it out.
Everyone shouts 'Melt!' or 'Set!' as fast as they can.
Turn the card over and read the back. The first player with the right answer keeps the card.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most cards wins. Playing alone, sort the cards into two piles and check the backs.

setup.art: A pile of small cards face down, and two children ready to shout.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the cards. Put them face down.

setup.art: A child turning over a card that says 'Kulfi dripping down its stick on a hot day', and another child shouting 'Melt!'
setup.caption: 2. Turn over a card. Shout 'Melt!' or 'Set!'

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards together. 2. Shuffle them. 3. Read the rules out loud.
flow.say: Melt means a solid is turning into a liquid. Set means a liquid is turning into a solid. Listen to each card and shout the right word.
flow.kid: Melt means solid to liquid. Set means liquid to solid. Shuffle the cards.

flow.do: 1. Take turns reading a card. 2. Everyone shouts. 3. Read the back and give the card to the winner.
flow.say: Hot red lava turning into black rock. Melt or set? Why?
flow.kid: Read a card out loud. Shout 'Melt!' or 'Set!' Check the back.

ask.q: Why is lava setting into rock a 'set' card?
good: Lava is a liquid, and it turns into solid rock.
It cools down and goes hard.

flow.parent: The lava and hailstone cards surprise many children. Lava is rock that has melted. Hailstones are balls of ice.

flow.do: 1. Put all the 'Melt' cards in one pile. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the 'Melt' cards. What made each one melt?
flow.kid: Look at the Melt cards. What made each one melt?

ask.q: What do all the 'Melt' cards have in common?
good: Something warm made them melt.
They all got warmer.

games.title: Room, Hand, Flame or Furnace? a sorting game
games.context: This is a sorting game about melting points. Each card names a solid. You put it under the place where it would melt: a warm room, your warm hand, a flame, or a furnace.

printables.title: The four-column board, drawn on a big sheet of paper

items.f: An ice cube
items.b: A warm room. Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius.

items.f: Ice cream
items.b: A warm room. It is mostly frozen milk and water.

items.f: A hailstone
items.b: A warm room. A hailstone is a ball of ice.

items.f: Coconut oil set hard in winter
items.b: A warm room. It melts at about 24 degrees Celsius.

items.f: Kulfi
items.b: A warm room. Kulfi is frozen milk.

items.f: A square of chocolate
items.b: Your warm hand. Chocolate melts a little below the warmth of your body.

items.f: Butter from the fridge
items.b: Your warm hand. Butter melts a little below the warmth of your body.

items.f: Ghee set hard on a cold day
items.b: Your warm hand. Ghee softens and melts as it warms.

items.f: Candle wax
items.b: Near a flame. Most candle wax melts at around 45 to 70 degrees Celsius.

img.credit: Kansieelina, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.f: A wax crayon
items.b: Near a flame. Crayons are made of wax and colour.

items.f: Beeswax
items.b: Near a flame. Honeybees make this wax for their honeycomb.

items.f: An iron nail
items.b: A furnace. Iron melts at about 1,500 degrees Celsius.

items.f: A steel spoon
items.b: A furnace. Steel is mostly iron.

items.f: A gold bangle
items.b: A furnace. Goldsmiths melt gold at about 1,060 degrees Celsius.

items.f: A glass bottle
items.b: A furnace. Glass is made by melting sand in a furnace.

items.f: A stone
items.b: A furnace, or deep inside the Earth. Melted rock is called lava when it comes out of a volcano.

rules: Draw the board: a big sheet split into four columns, with the labels at the top.
Shuffle the 16 cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. Turn over a card, read it, and put it in a column. Say why.
Turn the card over and read the back. If you were right, score one point. If not, move it to the right column.
When all 16 are placed, the player with the most points wins. Playing alone, try to beat your own score next time.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper with four columns labelled warm room, warm hand, flame and furnace, with a pile of cards beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the board. Shuffle the cards.

setup.art: A child placing a card that says 'A square of chocolate' in the warm hand column.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over a card. Put it in a column. Say why.

flow.do: 1. Draw the board with your child. 2. Cut out the cards. 3. Read the four labels together.
flow.say: Every solid melts somewhere. Some need only a warm room. Some need a furnace, which is a fire far hotter than a kitchen.
flow.kid: Draw the four columns. Read the labels. Cut out the cards.

flow.do: 1. Take turns turning over a card. 2. The player puts it in a column and says why. 3. Read the back and score.
flow.say: A gold bangle. Would it melt in your hand? Near a candle? Where would it melt? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Turn over a card. Where would it melt? Put it in a column.

ask.q: Why did you put chocolate in the 'warm hand' column?
good: It melts in my mouth and my hand.
It melted in the warm water in our race.

flow.parent: Many children put the stone or the steel spoon in 'never'. Explain that rock and metal do melt if they get hot enough.

flow.do: 1. Look at the board together. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the four columns. Which solids from our melting race can you find? Did they melt where the board says?
flow.kid: Find the solids from your melting race. Are they in the right place?

ask.q: Is there anything that would never melt, however hot it got?
good: I am not sure.
Even rock melts in a volcano.

projects.title: Make Your Own Ice Lollies
projects.context: In this project you freeze juice into ice lollies, with a cup of plain water beside them to compare. The next day you take them out and watch them melt as you eat them.

materials.item: three small steel cups or paper cups
fruit juice, nimbu pani or rose milk, enough for two cups
plain water for one cup
three ice cream sticks or steel teaspoons, for handles
space in the freezer
a bowl of warm water

schedule.what: Fill two cups with juice and one with plain water. Put a stick in each and freeze overnight.
Take out the lollies. Dip each cup in warm water to loosen it. Compare the plain ice and the juice lolly. Eat and watch them melt.

projects.record: Draw your ice lolly before and after five minutes out of the freezer.

setup.art: Three small steel cups, two filled with orange juice and one with plain water, each with a stick standing in it.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the cups. Put a stick in each.

setup.art: A grown-up dipping a steel cup into a bowl of warm water, and a child pulling out an orange ice lolly by the stick.
setup.caption: 2. The next day, dip each cup in warm water. Pull out the lolly.

setup.art: A child holding a melting ice lolly with drips running down the stick.
setup.caption: 3. Eat it, and watch where it melts first.

flow.do: 1. Your child pours juice into two cups and plain water into one. 2. Put a stick in each. 3. Put them in the freezer. 4. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Which will be harder tomorrow, the plain water or the juice? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pour juice in two cups and water in one. Add sticks. Which will be harder?

ask.q: Which will freeze harder? Why?
good: The water, because it is just water.
The juice, because it is thicker.

flow.wait: Leave them in the freezer overnight.
flow.parent: If the sticks fall over, freeze the cups for an hour first, then push the sticks in.

flow.do: 1. Take the cups out. 2. Dip each cup in warm water for about 10 seconds. 3. Pull out the lollies by the sticks. 4. Your child presses the plain ice and a juice lolly with a fingernail.
flow.say: Press each one with your nail. Which is harder? Now eat your lolly. Where does it start to melt?
flow.kid: Press each one with your nail. Which is harder? Where does it melt first?

ask.q: Why did the warm water help the lolly come out?
good: It melted the outside a little.
The ice next to the cup melted first.

ask.q: Which was harder?
good: The plain ice was harder.
The juice lolly was softer.

flow.parent: The juice lolly is usually a little softer, because the sugar in the juice makes water harder to freeze. The outside melts first, because it touches the warm air and your warm mouth.

challenges.title: The Slow-Melt Challenge: keep an ice cube solid for longest
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You wrap an ice cube to keep it from melting for as long as you can. Then you compare it with an ice cube left bare on a plate.
challenges.problem: Make an ice cube last as long as possible in a warm room. After one hour, the biggest ice cube left wins.
constraints: You may not put it back in the freezer or the fridge.
Use one ice cube for each wrap, the same size as the bare one.
materials: ice cubes of the same size
newspaper, a cotton cloth, a woollen sock, aluminium foil, a steel tumbler with a lid, a plastic box
a steel plate for the bare ice cube
a clock or a phone timer
general: Wrap the ice cube in a thick layer of newspaper.
Put it in a woollen sock, then in a closed tumbler.
creative: Use many layers: foil, then cloth, then newspaper, so warmth from the room has to pass through all of them.
Put the wrapped ice cube inside a closed plastic box, with crumpled newspaper packed round it.
challenges.your_turn: Think of your own wrap. Test it next to a bare ice cube for one hour. Which ice cube was bigger at the end? How could you make your wrap better?

setup.art: A row of ice cubes being wrapped in newspaper, a woollen sock and a cloth, and one bare ice cube on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. Wrap an ice cube your own way. Leave one bare.

setup.art: A clock showing one hour later, and a child unwrapping a newspaper bundle to find an ice cube still inside.
setup.caption: 2. After one hour, unwrap it. How big is it now?

flow.do: 1. Read the problem together. 2. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: An ice cube melts because warmth from the room goes into it. How could you slow the warmth down?
flow.kid: Warmth from the room melts ice. How could you slow it down?

ask.q: What could you wrap it in? Why?
good: A woollen sock, because wool keeps things warm or cold.
Lots of newspaper.

flow.do: 1. Your child wraps one ice cube. 2. Put one bare ice cube on a plate beside it. 3. Start a timer for one hour.
flow.say: Wrap your ice cube. Put the bare one next to it. Which will be bigger after an hour? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Wrap your ice cube. Put a bare one next to it. Start the timer.

flow.do: 1. After one hour, unwrap the ice cube. 2. Put it next to what is left of the bare one. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Which one is bigger? What did your wrap do? How could you make it even better?
flow.kid: Unwrap your ice cube. Is it bigger than the bare one?

ask.q: Why did the wrapped ice cube last longer?
good: The wrap slowed the warmth from getting in.
The air could not touch it.

flow.parent: A thick wrap slows the warmth from the room getting into the ice. A woollen sock keeps ice cold for the same reason it keeps feet warm: it slows warmth moving through it.

challenges.title: Chocolate Shapes: melt it, shape it, set it
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. You melt chocolate in warm water, pour the chocolate into a mould you choose, and let the chocolate set in a new shape.
challenges.problem: Make a chocolate in a shape of your own, using only things from your kitchen as a mould.
constraints: Melt the chocolate only in a bowl of warm water, never on the flame.
Your mould must be clean and from home.
materials: a small steel bowl, floated in a bigger bowl of hot water from a grown-up
moulds: an ice tray, bottle caps, a steel spoon, a small katori, a sheet of butter paper
general: Pour the melted chocolate into an ice tray to make little blocks.
Drip it onto butter paper in the shape of a letter.
creative: Pour a thin layer into a katori, let it set, then add a second layer, to make stripes.
Press a nut into each one before it sets.
challenges.your_turn: Choose your own mould and shape. How long did it take to set in the fridge? Did it come out in the shape of the mould?

setup.art: A small steel bowl of chocolate pieces floating in a wider bowl of steaming water, being stirred.
setup.caption: 1. Melt the chocolate in a bowl floated on hot water.

setup.art: A child spooning runny chocolate into the squares of an ice tray.
setup.caption: 2. Pour it into your mould.

setup.art: Chocolate blocks popped out of an ice tray, each the shape of one square.
setup.caption: 3. Set it in the fridge. Pop it out.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up fills a wide bowl with hot water. 2. Float a small steel bowl of broken chocolate on it. 3. Your child stirs until it is runny.
flow.say: The hot water melts the chocolate gently. Stir it slowly. Why do we not put it straight on the flame?
flow.kid: Stir the chocolate slowly. Watch it turn runny.

ask.q: Why melt it in warm water, not on the flame?
good: The flame is too hot and could burn it.
Chocolate needs only a little warmth to melt.

flow.parent: Keep water out of the chocolate, or it goes thick and lumpy. Chocolate burns easily on a direct flame.

flow.do: 1. Your child chooses a mould. 2. They spoon the melted chocolate into it. 3. Put it in the fridge.
flow.say: Pour it in. The liquid takes the shape of the mould. What shape will it be when it sets?
flow.kid: Spoon the chocolate into your mould. Put it in the fridge.
flow.wait: Leave it in the fridge for 30 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Take out the mould after 30 minutes. 2. Your child pops out the chocolate. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Did it set? What shape is it now? Is it still chocolate?
flow.kid: Pop out your chocolate. What shape is it? Is it still chocolate?

ask.q: Why did the chocolate set in the fridge?
good: It cooled down and solidified.
The fridge took the warmth out.

flow.parent: The chocolate may look a little dull or streaky. That is its fat setting in a new pattern, and it is still good chocolate.

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: a solid turns into a liquid
a liquid turns into a solid
solidify in the cold, like water into ice
the warmth at which a solid melts
items.why: These are the four main words of this unit.

items.p: In the melting race, which solid did not melt in the warm water, and needed a candle flame?
opts: The chocolate
The candle wax
The butter
items.why: Wax melts at a much higher warmth than bath water. Picking chocolate may mean mixing up the warm water step with the plate step.
items.context: This question is about the melting race. You put an ice cube, chocolate, butter, coconut oil and candle wax on a steel plate, then in a bowl of warm water, then near a candle flame.

items.p: Sort these into melting and solidifying.
items: kulfi dripping on a hot day
ghee going hard on a cold morning
butter going runny in a hot pan
water turning into ice in a tray
an ice cube shrinking in a glass of buttermilk
a drop of candle wax turning white on a plate
items.why: Melting is a solid turning into a liquid as it warms. Solidifying is a liquid turning into a solid as it cools.

items.p: Draw your square of chocolate before the warm water and after the warm water.
items.a: A square with sharp corners, then a flat, runny puddle in a katori.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the square shape before and a runny puddle after, with a label such as 'melted'.
items.context: This question is about the melting race. You put an ice cube, chocolate, butter, coconut oil and candle wax on a steel plate, then in a bowl of warm water, then near a candle flame.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, labelled before and after.

items.p: All solids melt at the same warmth.
items.why: False. In the melting race, the coconut oil melted in the room, the chocolate needed warm water, and the wax needed a flame.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why does your hand feel cold when you hold an ice cube?
items.a: Warmth from my hand goes into the ice to melt it, so my hand loses warmth and feels cold.
items.why: A strong answer says the warmth moves from the hand into the ice. Saying 'cold goes into my hand' is a common idea, but scientists describe warmth moving the other way.

items.p: Farhan put 5 solids on a plate: ice, coconut oil, butter, chocolate and wax. After 10 minutes, 2 had started to melt. How many still looked hard?
items.why: 5 take away 2 is 3. In a warm room, the ice and coconut oil usually start to melt first, and the butter, chocolate and wax still look hard.
items.context: This question is about the melting race. You put an ice cube, chocolate, butter, coconut oil and candle wax on a steel plate, then in a bowl of warm water, then near a candle flame.

items.p: Label each picture: melting or solidifying.
labels: a candle with a clear pool round its wick
an ice lolly being made in a freezer
a snowman shrinking in the sun
items.why: The flame melts the wax, the freezer freezes the juice, and the sun melts the snow.

items.p: Kavya and her grandmother, Paati, find a bar of chocolate that melted in a bag and then went hard again with white streaks on top.

views.says: It has gone bad. We should throw it away.
It is still chocolate. It only melted and set again.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Paati, because melting can be undone and the chocolate is the same substance. It also says Kavya is right that it looks different, and that food left in a dirty or wet place can spoil.
items.why: Melting and setting again does not turn chocolate into something else. The white streaks are its fat, set in a new pattern. Kavya is right to check food before eating it.

items.p: Three of these melt in a warm room or a warm hand. Which one does not?
opts: Butter
An ice cube
A steel spoon
Chocolate
items.why: Steel melts only in a furnace, far hotter than any home. The other three melt in a warm room or a warm hand.

items.p: Put these in order, from the one that melts most easily to the one that needs the most warmth.
items.why: Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius, chocolate a little below body warmth, candle wax near a flame, and iron only in a furnace.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: in the fridge, the melted chocolate went hard but the water did not. Why?
items.a: The fridge is cold enough to make chocolate solidify, but water needs the freezer, which is much colder.
items.why: A strong answer says each liquid solidifies at its own warmth, and water needs more cold than chocolate.
items.context: This question is about the melting race. You put an ice cube, chocolate, butter, coconut oil and candle wax on a steel plate, then in a bowl of warm water, then near a candle flame.

items.p: Lakshmi's coconut oil is golden and runny in Kochi, but white and hard on a January morning in Delhi. Why?
opts: The oil went bad on the train
Delhi is colder than the oil's melting point that morning
Delhi oil is a different oil
items.why: Coconut oil melts at about 24 degrees Celsius. A Delhi winter morning is colder than that, so the oil solidifies. Picking 'went bad' is what Lakshmi's Appa thought at first.

items.p: When liquid wax cools and turns hard, we say it ____.
items.why: Solidifying is a liquid turning into a solid as it cools.

items.p: In the freezer watch, the ice started at the top and the sides. Why did the middle freeze last?
items.a: The top touches the cold air and the sides touch the cold cup, so they lose their warmth first. The middle is furthest from the cold.
items.why: A strong answer says that water freezes first where it loses warmth first.
items.context: This question is about the freezer watch. You put the same water in a steel tumbler and a plastic tumbler in the freezer, and look every 30 minutes.

items.p: Nila and Bidisha want to cool a glass of nimbu pani on a hot day in Kolkata.

views.says: Put ice cubes in it. The ice will cool it quickly as it melts.
Put the glass in the fridge. Then the drink won't get watery.

items.ask: Whose plan would you choose? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one with a reason, such as 'melting ice takes in a lot of warmth, so it cools fast'. It also says what the other plan gets right, such as 'the drink stays strong and not watery'.
items.why: Both plans have a real point. Melting ice takes warmth from the drink fast, but adds water. The fridge is slower but keeps the taste.

items.p: Draw a tumbler of water in the freezer after one hour. Colour where the ice has formed.
items.a: A thin layer of ice on top and a ring of ice round the sides, with water still in the middle.
items.why: A strong drawing shows ice on top and at the sides, where the water touches the cold air and the cold cup.
items.context: This question is about the freezer watch. You put the same water in a steel tumbler and a plastic tumbler in the freezer, and look every 30 minutes.
items.art: An empty outline of a tumbler.

items.p: When water freezes into ice, it turns into a different substance.
items.why: False. Ice is still water, as a solid. Melt it, and it is liquid water again.

items.p: Draw a line from each solid to where it would melt.
items.why: Each substance has its own melting point. Gold needs a goldsmith's furnace, at about 1,060 degrees Celsius.

items.p: This drawing shows a lit candle. Label the solid wax, the liquid wax and the flame.
labels: the clear pool round the wick
a: the hard white candle: solid wax
items.why: The flame's warmth melts the wax just below it into a clear liquid. The rest of the candle stays solid, because it is further from the flame.

items.p: Revathi made 4 ice lollies. She ate 1 on Monday and 1 on Tuesday. On Wednesday she made 2 more. How many lollies does she have now?
items.why: 4 take away 2 is 2. Then 2 more makes 4.

items.p: Three of these are solidifying. Which one is melting?
opts: Lava turning into black rock
Hot jaggery syrup setting into chikki
Snow turning into a stream
Water turning into ice
items.why: Snow turning into a stream is melting: a solid turning into a liquid. The other three are liquids turning into solids.

items.p: Many people think hot water can never freeze faster than cold water. A Tanzanian schoolboy, Erasto Mpemba, said it did. How could you test it at home?
items.a: Put the same amount of hot water and cold water in two same tumblers, side by side in the freezer. Look every 30 minutes to see which one freezes first.
items.why: A strong answer keeps everything the same except how hot the water starts. Scientists still argue about this, so any honest result is useful.

items.p: Why do we melt chocolate in a bowl floating on warm water, and not straight on the flame?
opts: Chocolate melts with only a little warmth, and a flame can burn it
Chocolate never melts on a flame
Warm water makes more chocolate
items.why: Chocolate melts a little below the warmth of your body, so warm water is enough. A direct flame is far hotter, and the chocolate can burn.

A liquid turning into a solid

Freezing
Boiling

quiz.p: Which of these needs the most warmth to melt?
opts: An ice cube
Butter
An iron nail
quiz.why: Iron melts at about 1,500 degrees Celsius, in a furnace. Ice and butter melt in a warm room or a warm hand.

quiz.p: Mina floats a piece of candle wax and a square of chocolate in bath-warm water. After five minutes, what does she see?
opts: The chocolate is runny and the wax is still hard
Both are runny
The wax is runny and the chocolate is still hard
quiz.why: Chocolate melts at a little below body warmth, so bath water melts it. Wax needs more warmth than bath water gives.
quiz.context: This question is about the melting race. You put an ice cube, chocolate, butter, coconut oil and candle wax on a steel plate, then in a bowl of warm water, then near a candle flame.

quiz.p: Melted chocolate is put in the fridge for 20 minutes. What happens?
opts: It stays runny
It solidifies and is still chocolate
It turns into a new food
quiz.why: Chocolate solidifies as it cools, and it is still chocolate. Melting can be undone.

quiz.p: Anjali holds an ice cube in her hand in Pune. Why does her hand feel cold?
opts: Cold flows out of the ice into her hand
Warmth flows out of her hand into the ice
The ice is wet
quiz.why: Warmth always flows from the warmer thing to the cooler thing. Her hand loses warmth to melt the ice.

quiz.p: Why does a glass of buttermilk get colder when you add ice?
opts: The ice takes warmth from the buttermilk to melt
The ice adds cold to the buttermilk
The buttermilk turns into ice
quiz.why: Melting ice takes in a lot of warmth from what is around it. That warmth comes out of the buttermilk, so it cools down.

quiz.p: Coconut oil is runny in Chennai but white and hard on a cold Delhi morning. Which is true?
opts: It is the same oil in both places
The Delhi oil has gone bad
Only Chennai oil is real coconut oil
quiz.why: Coconut oil melts at about 24 degrees Celsius. Above that it is a liquid, below it a solid. It is the same oil.

quiz.p: Meenakshi guessed the ice would melt last. Then she watched it melting on the plate. What should she do?
opts: Say her guess was right anyway
Say what she saw, and change her idea
Stop the test
quiz.why: A good scientist guesses first, then says what the test really showed. A wrong guess is how we learn.

quiz.p: In a tumbler of water in the freezer, where does the ice usually start?
opts: At the top and round the sides
In the very middle
Nowhere, it all freezes at once
quiz.why: The top and sides touch the cold air and the cold cup, so they lose their warmth first.
quiz.context: This question is about the freezer watch. You put the same water in a steel tumbler and a plastic tumbler in the freezer, and look every 30 minutes.

applications: Goldsmiths melt gold and pour it into moulds to make ornaments, and it solidifies in the new shape.
Candle makers melt old wax and pour it into moulds with a wick, where it sets into new candles.
Kulfi makers pour sweet milk into metal cones and pack them in ice mixed with salt, which is colder than plain ice, so the kulfi freezes.
Steel and iron are melted in huge furnaces and poured into moulds. When they solidify, they are rolled and cut into rails, beams and sheets.
Ice keeps fish fresh on boats and at fish markets, from Kochi to Kolkata, because melting ice takes in warmth.
In Ladakh, the engineer Chewang Norphel built artificial glaciers: shallow pools where water freezes in winter and melts slowly in spring, to water the fields.

open_questions.why_open: People once said our weight melts the ice. Scientists worked out that this is too small to explain it. Most think the surface of ice has a very thin wet layer of its own, but they still argue about how it forms and how much it matters.

open_questions.q: Can hot water freeze faster than cold water?
open_questions.why_open: Erasto Mpemba, a schoolboy in Tanzania, saw it happen in 1963. Some tests since then have found the same, and some have not. Scientists still do not agree on whether it really happens, or why.

open_questions.q: How does the very first bit of ice start in water?
open_questions.why_open: Very clean, still water can stay liquid below 0 degrees Celsius for a while. Ice needs a tiny starting point, such as a speck of dust. Scientists are still studying exactly how that first tiny crystal forms.

maths.problem: In the melting race, Kavya's coconut oil was all runny after 6 minutes. Her ice cube took 30 minutes to melt. How many more minutes did the ice take?
maths.explain: 30 take away 6 is 24. So the ice took 24 more minutes than the coconut oil, even though ice melts at a lower warmth. A whole ice cube needs a lot of warmth to melt.
maths.context: This question is about the melting race. You put an ice cube, chocolate, butter, coconut oil and candle wax on a steel plate, then in a bowl of warm water, then near a candle flame.
maths.why_maths: Taking away shows how much longer one solid took, which tells us something surprising about ice.

maths.problem: Priya checks her plate every 2 minutes for 10 minutes. How many times does she look? If she looks every 5 minutes instead, how many times does she look?
maths.answer: 5 times every 2 minutes, and 2 times every 5 minutes.
maths.explain: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 is 5 looks. 5, 10 is 2 looks. Looking more often means she can say more exactly when each solid started to melt.
maths.context: This question is about the melting race. You put an ice cube, chocolate, butter, coconut oil and candle wax on a steel plate, then in a bowl of warm water, then near a candle flame.
maths.why_maths: Counting in twos and fives shows that looking more often gives us a better record of when things change.

maths.problem: In the melting race, ice and coconut oil melted in the room, chocolate and butter in the warm water, and wax near the flame. Make a tally of how many melted in each place. Which place melted the most?
maths.answer: Room: 2. Warm water: 2. Flame: 1. The room and the warm water tied, with 2 each.
maths.explain: Each solid goes in the place where it first melted. The wax is the only one that needed a flame, so it stands out.
maths.context: This question is about the melting race. You put an ice cube, chocolate, butter, coconut oil and candle wax on a steel plate, then in a bowl of warm water, then near a candle flame.
maths.why_maths: Sorting and tallying shows the pattern of the race at a glance.

maths.problem: Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius. Your body is about 37 degrees. Coconut oil melts at about 24 degrees. Is coconut oil's melting point nearer to ice or to your body?
maths.answer: Nearer to your body. 37 take away 24 is 13. 24 take away 0 is 24. 13 is less than 24.
maths.explain: The gap from 24 to 37 is 13 degrees, and the gap from 0 to 24 is 24 degrees. So coconut oil melts at a warmth closer to your body, which is why your warm finger melted it in the story.
maths.why_maths: Comparing numbers tells us which solids will melt on a warm day and which will stay hard.

roots.context: We have raced five solids, melted them and set them again in the fridge. Now we ask what that tells us about the things around us, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In your race, ice and coconut oil melted in the room, and chocolate in warm water. Wax melted only near a flame. Each substance changes between solid and liquid at its own warmth. Whether a thing is a solid or a liquid depends on how warm it is.
deep_truth.habit: We call butter, wax and ice solids, and water and oil liquids, as if that were part of what each thing is. The race showed the same chocolate as a solid and then a liquid, and the only thing that changed was its warmth.
deep_truth.evidence: In the melting race, the coconut oil melted on the plate, the chocolate and butter melted in bath-warm water, and the wax melted only beside a candle flame. In the fridge, the chocolate, butter and oil set hard again, while the water needed the freezer.

three.who_am_i: Your body is about 37 degrees Celsius. That is warm enough to melt chocolate on your tongue and butter in your hand.
three.what_is_life: Honeybees make wax inside their own bodies, and build their honeycomb from it. The wax stays solid in a hot hive because it melts only at a much higher warmth.
three.what_is_this_world: The same water is ice on the Himalayas in winter, and a river in the plains in summer. Rock melts deep inside the Earth and comes out of volcanoes as lava.

roots.thread: Ice, chocolate, wax and iron look very different. Yet each one is a solid when cool and a liquid when warm enough, and the change goes both ways. Each has its own warmth for the change. So in one warm room, ice melts, coconut oil is runny and wax stays hard. Everything is conscious, down to these tiny particles.

teachings.teaching: Heraclitus, a thinker from ancient Greece, said that everything flows and nothing stays still. He said you cannot step into the same river twice.
teachings.link: A river keeps its name while its water keeps changing. Coconut oil keeps its name too, whether it is hard and white in Delhi or runny and golden in Kochi.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha taught that all things that are made up of parts and causes do not last forever. Seeing this clearly makes us suffer less.
teachings.link: A solid stays solid only while it stays cool enough. Warm it, and its shape goes. The melting race showed that each solid lasts only as long as its warmth allows.

teachings.teaching: Nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water. Yet nothing is better at wearing away what is hard and strong.
teachings.link: Hard ice and soft water are the same water. The Tao Te Ching, from China, praises the soft, flowing state that hard things can melt into.

science.text: Pure water freezes and ice melts at the same temperature, 0 degrees Celsius. Every pure substance melts and solidifies at its own fixed temperature.
Why ice is slippery, and whether hot water can freeze faster than cold, are still argued about by scientists.

other_view.view: They say a melting ice cube has no awareness at all. They explain melting fully by particles moving faster as they warm up, and they find no need for a mind to explain it.

science: Melting points: water 0 degrees Celsius; coconut oil about 24 degrees; butter about 32 to 35 degrees; cocoa butter in chocolate about 34 to 36 degrees; paraffin candle wax about 45 to 70 degrees; beeswax about 62 to 64 degrees; gold about 1,064 degrees; iron about 1,538 degrees. Standard reference values.

Joseph Black's ice and water experiment, around 1761, Glasgow: ice took about ten hours to melt and warm, where the same water warmed as much in about half an hour. Britannica, 'Joseph Black'; Black's Lectures on the Elements of Chemistry (1803).
E. B. Mpemba and D. G. Osborne, 'Cool?', Physics Education 4 (1969). Later disagreement: for example H. C. Burridge and P. F. Linden, Scientific Reports (2016).

Ice slipperiness: pressure melting is too small to explain it; a premelted liquid-like surface layer is the common view, still debated (for example R. Rosenberg, 'Why is ice slippery?', Physics Today, 2005).
Salt lowers the freezing point of water, so ice and salt make a mixture colder than 0 degrees Celsius. Used by traditional kulfi makers.
Chocolate bloom: white streaks on chocolate that has melted and set again are cocoa butter crystals in a different form (fat bloom).
Chewang Norphel's artificial glaciers in Ladakh, built from 1987 onwards.

playtest: Thought through as a parent and child in a flat. The melting race uses things most homes have: an ice cube, a square from any chocolate bar, butter or ghee, coconut oil and a candle. Half a teaspoon of fridge-hard coconut oil goes runny within about 10 minutes in a room above 24 degrees Celsius, which is most Indian homes for most of the year. A note covers a cold room. Bath-warm water, about 40 degrees, melts chocolate and butter in small floating steel katoris within a few minutes, but is below the melting point of paraffin wax, so the wax stays hard. A lit candle makes a clear pool within two or three minutes. In 20 minutes in the fridge, the thin layers of chocolate, butter and oil set, while the water stays liquid. The freezer watch takes 2 to 4 hours, with short looks. The spine is the intro, the chocolate tongue test and the melting race (session 1, about 40 minutes), then the explanations, Roots and the quiz (session 2, about 30 minutes). This leads on from the solids, liquids and gases unit, whose experiments use pouring and an ice glove, and it does not repeat them.
